description: External supporting evidence. These sources were opened during the Evidence Engine v2 work on 2026-11-11. They are NOT Study Library studies and are kept in a separate register.

sources.short_label: NASA HRP evidence report (Rivas et al. 2023)
sources.citation: Rivas E, Strock N, Dillon EL, Frisco D. Risk of Impaired Performance Due to Reduced Muscle Mass, Strength & Endurance (Short Title: Muscle) and Risk of Reduced Physical Performance Capabilities Due to Reduced Aerobic Capacity (Short Title: Aerobic). NASA Human Research Program evidence report HRP-47072; NASA Technical Reports Server document 20220019338; published 1 April 2023.
sources.access: Full PDF (169 pages) downloaded from NTRS and read as text.
sources.population: Spaceflight (review of Mercury through ISS) and ground analogues; this register uses only its spaceflight statements.
used_for: 8-day Space Shuttle (STS-47) MRI muscle-volume changes, used as short-duration points in the muscle-size duration chart.
Statement that long-duration loss was greater than short-duration loss but less than short flights would predict.
Its description of Gopalakrishnan et al. (2010), used to interpret the ambiguous calf range in the abstract.

quotes.text: The subjects included four Space Shuttle crewmembers from an 8-day mission. All subjects completed three preflight measurements and two postflight tests at R+1 and R+15/16.
Significant reductions were observed in the anterior calf muscles (−3.9%), the gastrocnemius/soleus muscles (−6.3%), hamstrings (−8.0%), and intrinsic back muscles (−10.3%) [14].

The data indicated that loss of muscle volume, particularly in the legs and back, was greater during long-duration space flight than with short-duration space flight, but not as great as the data from short-duration flight might have predicted [114].
One investigation during the “iRED era” involved four ISS astronauts with mission durations of 161–194 days [57]
Calf muscles were found to undergo the greater decrements than thigh muscles (10-18% vs. 4–7% loss, respectively) [57].

sources.limitations: Secondary source: the 8-day values are the report's summary of an earlier Shuttle experiment (its reference [14]), not the primary paper. No SD or CI is given. Measured at R+1, not landing day. The same report's Figure 16 caption gives n = 8 for the 8-day group while the text says four crew members; the text value is stored.

sources.short_label: Winnard et al. 2019 (bed rest, no countermeasures)
sources.citation: Winnard A, Scott J, Waters N, Vance M, Caplan N. Effect of Time on Human Muscle Outcomes During Simulated Microgravity Exposure Without Countermeasures—Systematic Review. Frontiers in Physiology 2019;10:1046.
sources.access: Open-access full text opened at frontiersin.org; the first 100,000 characters (through the main Discussion) were read.
sources.population: Ground analogue: bed-rest studies described as spaceflight simulations, no-countermeasure groups only. NOT spaceflight data.
used_for: Context shown beside the duration slider: in bed rest without countermeasures, muscle outcomes worsen over time and the largest changes are in plantar flexors and quadriceps. No number from this source enters any calculation.

quotes.text: The most common bed rest duration was 60 days, with shortest and longest durations being seven and 120 days, respectively.
Moderate effects were apparent by 7–15 days and large by 28–56 days.
All muscle volumes decreased over time. Moderate effects were becoming apparent by 14 days and large by 28 days.
The high risk of bias and lack of core outcome measure sets means that the conclusions reached by this review should be treated with some caution

sources.limitations: Reports days to reach moderate or large effect sizes, not percent change against time, so it cannot supply a time-course function. Bed rest is not spaceflight and these groups did no exercise.

sources.short_label: Marusic et al. 2021 (bed rest, abstract only)
sources.citation: Marusic U, Narici M, Simunic B, Pisot R, Ritzmann R. Nonuniform loss of muscle strength and atrophy during bed rest: a systematic review. Journal of Applied Physiology 2021;131(1):194–206.
sources.access: ABSTRACT ONLY, read through the Europe PMC record (PMID 33703945). The publisher and PubMed Central pages blocked automated access, so the full text and its fitted equations were not read.
sources.population: Ground analogue: bed rest, 318 healthy adults, 5–120 days, knee extensors. NOT spaceflight data.
used_for: Context only: its abstract states that knee-extensor strength loss and atrophy in bed rest follow a logarithmic pattern. This is a reason to distrust a straight line; it is not used to draw any curve because the equation was not read.

quotes.text: Bed rest results in nonuniform loss of isometric muscle strength and atrophy over time.

sources.limitations: Abstract-level only. No coefficients were read, so no function from this source is used.

sources.short_label: Comfort et al. 2021 (spaceflight meta-analysis, abstract only)
sources.citation: Comfort P, McMahon JJ, Jones PA, Cuthbert M, Kendall K, Lake JP, Haff GG. Effects of Spaceflight on Musculoskeletal Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, Considerations for Interplanetary Travel. Sports Medicine 2021;51(10):2097–2114.
sources.access: ABSTRACT ONLY, read through the Europe PMC record (PMID 34115344). The publisher page required sign-in and PubMed Central blocked automated access.
used_for: Context only: confirms that pooled spaceflight evidence shows large lower-limb strength and size deficits with high between-study heterogeneity. The abstract contains no analysis of mission duration, so nothing from it enters the duration model.
sources.limitations: Abstract-level only. Pooled effect sizes are standardized (Hedges' g), not percent changes, and are not used in any calculation.
